<a id="w121"></a>

W121 · Immediate read after successful fsync returns the previous file's payload

Class/state: normal-operation data correctness; OPEN, October16,2026. On fa29f9277 ORCD native RDMA/direct, .efs enabled, expiry disabled: seven clients, eight writers and two query threads each. Unique512-byte file: create/write/fsync/close, exact readback, unlink. Four90s rounds reproduced255 mismatches in123,932 cycles, although all write/fsync/close and unlink operations returned success. Both unmodified devel and the restored queued-read-vote candidate fail; this is not isolated to that scheduling change. Examples return the prior file's512-byte value.

Diagnosis/gate, October 16: correct bytes reach the FUSE reply, but concurrent fork causes stale application buffers on ORCD's unpinned FUSE kernel read path. Fixed-file reproduction: 86,629/433,368 failures with fork, 0/486,164 with posix_spawn. The installed module uses iov_iter_get_pages2; upstream fix 738adade96b2 pins these pages. Kernel remediation is deferred by the user; W121 remains OPEN. Isolate query subprocesses from reader address spaces for performance experiments, without treating that workaround as application correctness acceptance. Require a fixed-kernel fork/read rerun plus original mixed load, peer and clean-restart checks. Diagnosis and regression. Unplanned recovery remains deferred. Reproduction, source identities and results.

<a id="w122"></a>

W122 · Discoverable effective settings for efsd, efs-fuse and the portal

Class/state: product observability feature; PROPOSED, October 16, 2026. Requested for the stable beta product. This item records the feature; backend implementation and end-to-end acceptance are NOTRUN. It does not restore archived experimental features or enable expiry.

Problem: binary help lists command-line options and efs-mgmt offers individual status/policy commands, but there is no complete machine-readable catalog of supported startup settings and runtime controls, or their effective values. The portal's process argument/environment probe can show explicit launch overrides only. An unset variable is not proof of a disabled feature; version defaults, normalization and later policy changes remain invisible. The current portal Settings draft is partial observability, not completion.

Proposed behavior:

  • Maintain role-specific catalogs for efsd and efs-fuse, shared by help, validation and introspection where practical. Include CLI options, supported environment settings and existing mutable runtime policies. Do not expose fault-injection controls as supported beta configuration.
  • Provide a versioned JSON interface, provisionally efs-mgmt settings --json, identifying the target process/role and build. Daemon lookup and FUSE-client lookup need distinct explicit targets: the daemon cannot infer client state. Define an authenticated/authorized read-only client introspection mechanism independent of whether .efs commands are enabled.
  • For every supported setting report name, description, type, unit, valid range/choices, build-specific default, effective value, value source and applicability. Sources distinguish CLI, environment, default and runtime policy. Report restart/remount-required versus live-changeable, and identify any existing supported setter without adding a universal mutation endpoint.
  • Read normalized active state rather than presenting environment text as effective configuration. Mark unavailable, unsupported, redacted and unset states distinctly. Never disclose credentials or arbitrary environment data.
  • Near the bottom of the portal, show a read-only Settings section with a process selector, daemon/client scope, build identity and observation time. Distinguish stale/disconnected data and mixed builds. Keep a clearly labelled partial fallback for older binaries; never invent defaults for them.

Acceptance gates: catalog coverage of supported startup/runtime controls; CLI/environment precedence and validation; defaults versus explicit overrides; normalized/effective values; live policy updates; restart/remount semantics; separate daemon and client targets; disabled .efs; access denial/redaction; mixed/older builds; stale portal observations. Run focused integration on AMD or Intel with a small cluster and two clients; ORCD scale is not required. No live configuration editor or automatic rollout is included in this item.

<a id="w123"></a>

W123 — Automatic crash recovery through per-file durable versions

New feature; proposed 2026-10-16. Design/ordering review first; implementation and acceptance NOTRUN. Recover committed state without node format/rebuild while retaining immediate visibility, grouped barriers and fsync guarantees. Related W71 stays open. Canonical feature plan and gates.

<a id="w124"></a>

W124 — Fast delete: quota at delete, batched reclaim and fragment slot reuse

Performance/capacity; proposed 2026-10-18. Design review first; implementation, private A/B and orcd-mini acceptance NOTRUN. POSIX delete stays metadata-only. Revised after design review: logical quota is credited exactly once when removal is final, with reclaim-pending bytes and physical availability (atomic per-filesystem reservations) reported separately. Reclaim moves from inode-at-a-time processing (2–3 proposals and ~8 fsyncs per inode) to bounded batches per owning group, with a journal-first node protocol (accepted for reclaim before the acknowledgement, physically reclaimed later). Rate targets are hypotheses for the A/B. Then small-file packing (W125). Slot reuse (needs reader retirement) and subtree delete are deferred. Motivated by 0.18–0.21 GiB/min reclaim and a 398 GiB-per-node backlog on orcd-mini. Canonical proposal and gates.

<a id="w125"></a>

W125 — Small-file packing by default (background packer)

Capacity/performance; proposed 2026-10-18; revised to background packing after close. Packing at close failed the early P1 measurement (close 5.4× slower, throughput −71 to −78%), so files are written exactly as today and an always-on background packer moves closed files below the threshold (initially 16 KiB) into shared segments of ordinary fragments (no data in metadata rows), lifetime-grouped by publication group, directory subtree and creation epoch, then retires their per-file fragments through W124's batched journal. Larger files keep per-file fragments. The same copy-forward engine compacts survivors of mostly-dead segments (bounded overhead ≤1/t). One write path and no switch that disables the packer: tag the last devel commit without it (archive/unpacked-small-files-<date>); comparisons build the tag. Existing small files are backfilled. Pieces ported from archive/packing-containers-20261016 (D37) without the client writer, cohorts, EFS_PACKED_WRITES or the container engine. Motivated by ~800× raw amplification for sub-KiB files on orcd-mini. Canonical proposal and gates · implementation plan.

<a id="w126"></a>

W126 — KV readers convoy behind exclusive LSM phases on a busy leader

Performance; opened 2026-10-21. Steps 1 and 3 deployed on orcd-mini (8fb4247ad, 2026-10-21 23:14Z). Lock-wait gate PASS; create-rate gate FAIL (no measurable gain; throughput is bounded elsewhere). Step 4 deferred. A/B evidence. Found under the user's 32M-file tiny_files.py run on orcd-mini 47ba6b590 (profile). From ~1.0 to ~2.6 M files, creates fell from 2,564 to 1,130 files/s. Over the same span, leader n1's LSM lock waits rose from 3.3% to 16–18% of its context switches.

  • About 93% of the read waits were LOOKUP → efs_meta_apply_getattr gets.
  • Apply's own blocked switches sat in pthread_rwlock_wrlock: 1,051 in a 3 s DWARF capture.
  • apply-sleep (>20 ms) occurred 1,400–2,600 times per ~90 s window, up to 400 ms.

Mechanism. Every KV read (point get or scan) shares one view_rw per node. The lock is writer-preferring so Raft apply cannot starve. Each exclusive acquisition (lsm_lock) therefore waits for every in-flight reader, including long scans, and new readers queue behind it. Both Raft groups share the node's KV, so W66's leader distribution alone does not remove this (h->mu plan).

Step 1 (implemented). Writer-owned flags and counters change only under mu, and readers only read them. A new lsm_peek_lock takes mu without view_rw for read-only peeks:

  • the failure-flag check before every batch's WAL append, which halves the exclusive phases per applied batch;
  • REPORT's efs_kv_lsm_l0_hot;
  • efs_kv_lsm_stats and seg_count;
  • the query-refresh revision reads (metadata_revisions, transaction_revision/activity, cleanup_deferred).

Peeks keep lsm_lock's fail-fast abort inside a read section. tests/test_kv_lsm.c test_peek_beside_reader parks a reader inside a scan callback and requires every peek to return. It FAILs on 47ba6b590 and PASSes with the change. On node9901, the patched tree passes test_kv_lsm, test_kv_lsm_concurrent 4, test_kv, test_meta_apply, test_raft_store, test_query_disk, test_txn, test_kv_snapshot_tail, test_kv_reader_gate and test_query_catalog.

Step 2 (folded into step 3). A flush of 100 ms or more logs kv-flush: files= io_ms= manifest_ms= view_yielded=. On orcd-mini, flushes wrote 26–37 L0 files with 117–160 ms of I/O each. Before step 3, all of that ran under the exclusive view.

Step 3 (8fb4247ad, implemented and deployed). After the pending merge the memtable is frozen, because every writer waits on mu. At the outermost writer level, kv_flush_locked therefore yields the exclusive view and keeps mu while it writes and fsyncs the L0 files, the MANIFEST and the WAL reset. It retakes the view only to publish the L0 slots and to clear the memtable. Between those two steps, readers find identical rows in both. The memtable still clears only after the MANIFEST write succeeds. test_kv_lsm and three runs of test_kv_lsm_concurrent 8 PASS.

Verification.

  • make test (scripts/make_test_summary.sh): 813/813 commands, 1 environmental failure (docs check without results/).
  • orcd-mini deploy and POSIX smoke: 216/216 PASS.
  • A/B (A 8fb, B 47ba, A' 8fb) with the user's exact tiny_files.py shape, at matched new-file counts:
    • leader LSM lock waits 1.6–6.0% vs 13.6% at 0.9 M, and 5.4% vs 20.9% at 1.7 M;
    • creates/s 736 / 598 / 551 at 0.9 M, which follows the run order, not the build.

The remaining leader waits are h->mu in host_pump, proposals and REPORT (h->mu plan), plus XFS log fsync waits.

Remaining. Step 4 (bound how long merge_scan holds the shared view) is deferred until LSM waits rise again. Create throughput on orcd-mini is not a W126 matter.

<a id="w127-w131-fix"></a>

W127–W131 apply hardening — implementation (October 22)

Implemented on claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087; not merged. One package, as the scope review asked:

  • EFS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED (-24) is the "unsupported or malformed encoding" class. Dispatch returns it for unknown tags and for reserved or retired tags; the DIR, SESSION and TXN decoders for unknown sub-tags and short frames; the other decoders for length and count errors. No normalization list in host_apply turns it into success. Business refusals (SALT mismatch, QUERY_POLICY CAS, the other ring verdicts) are unchanged, and group-routing mismatches still answer INVAL/PROTO.
  • On that result host_apply aborts the KV scope (no cursor), returns the error so the Raft core does not advance applied, and marks the group incompatible (sticky, separate from kv_incomplete): one diagnostic line with group, index, term, tag, sub-tag and length; step-down; no campaign; proposals and ReadIndex refused with EFS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED. A retried apply returns at once without dispatching.
  • W130: DIR returns IO/NOMEM so the per-index retry applies.
  • W131: no KV engine returns IO (logged once) instead of OK; the empty no-op entry still applies.

Evidence (node9901, gcc 11.5.0):

  • tests/test_apply_unsupported.py (wired): the production host_apply over a real KV LSM. An unsupported verdict on a normally-normalized tag leaves no row and no cursor, also after reopening the KV; the state is sticky; another group on the same KV still applies; a missing engine is refused; DIR storage errors retry; unknown or short DIR/TXN frames are unsupported. test_gc_verdict.py checks that no verdict list absorbs it.
  • scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh: a private 3-node TCP efsd set (ports 17631–17633). An entry with unknown tag 200 is committed to group 0; all replicas log the diagnostic and keep applied below it; group 0 has no leader and refuses a new MKFS; group 2 keeps its leader and stays applied; after restarting all nodes the same holds. PASS.

Remaining: RDMA and multi-host runs; the one-replica DIR fault injection (W130); cross-group and cached read refusal and a status-reply field (W66 B4); prevalidating batch members before the first side effect (they are rejected inside the aborted scope today). New finding: the proposal RPC accepts a tag this build does not know, so any connection can commit such an entry and halt a group. Submit-side refusal of unknown tags belongs with the W133 connection-state matrix.

Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the dead-code audit M1; FIXED on claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087 (not merged); unit and private 3-node gates PASS, RDMA/multi-host NOTRUN. host_apply_dispatch ends in return EFS_OK; (src/server/raft_host.c:3507). W129 — host_apply turns decoder errors into success and commits the cursor

Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit M3; FIXED on claude/dead-code-cleanup-5f7087 (not merged); unit gates PASS.

  • For about 45 command tags (raft_host.c:2941–2962), host_apply forces the result to EFS_OK whatever the apply returned. Only IO/NOMEM are restored (:2984–3000).
  • So a decoder EFS_ERR_PROTO (for example a wrong-length CREATE) commits the cursor and is skipped on every replica.
  • QUERY_POLICY (:2966), CREATE_REFUSAL/EXPIRY (:2967–2970) and nine SESSION sub-tags (:2975–2982) do the same.
  • tests/test_gc_verdict.py:75 asserts core_result(EFS_MD_CMD_APPEND_RES,EFS_ERR_PROTO,37)==EFS_OK, so the test suite currently protects this behaviour.

Not every PROTO is a decode failure. SALT answers PROTO for an anchor mismatch (:2933–2935), and QUERY_POLICY treats PROTO as a logical CAS verdict (:2963–2966). Both are legitimate business refusals.

Fix and gate:

  • Decoders return the W127 malformed/unsupported outcome. Business refusals, PROTO included where it means a refusal, stay ring verdicts.
  • Removing PROTO from one allow-list is not the fix.
  • Replace the expression-level check in test_gc_verdict.py with tests at the apply boundary: verdict, cursor and restart.

<a id="w133"></a>

W133 — Client protocol declaration gate is fail-open

Correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit P1; OPEN, fix NOTRUN.

  • Only INODE_GETCHUNKS, GET_SEGMENT and PUT_SEGMENT require CLIENT_HELLO (handler.c:186–190).
  • Every other request (PUT_CHUNK, namespace mutations, REPORT, …) is served on an undeclared connection.
  • The version check is >= EFS_PROTOCOL_MIN_VERSION (handler.c:196, src/common/protocol.c:697), so newer versions are accepted too.
  • scripts/w125_p3_compat.sh case 2 expects an old client's writes to keep working, which contradicts the no-backward-compatibility rule.

Fix and gate:

  • Require one exact supported declaration, defined as a connection-state and message matrix: client, peer (HELLO) and management connections have different valid operations, and the declaration messages themselves must be accepted.
  • Cover TCP and RDMA, reconnects and forwarding connections.
  • Test with synthetic unsupported and missing declarations.
  • Turn w125_p3_compat.sh into a refusal test or delete it.
  • A declaration is not authentication, and this item does not claim it.

<a id="w133-fix"></a> Implementation (October 22, branch devel-k04, not merged):

  • EFS_PROTOCOL_VERSION is 3, and EFS_PROTOCOL_MIN_VERSION is removed. Both sides require an exact match. A client also refuses a server that accepts it with another version.
  • efs_decl_gate_frame (src/common/protocol.c) runs on every frame in server_handle_conn before dispatch, on TCP and RDMA alike. Before an accepted CLIENT_HELLO only HEARTBEAT is served. Any other request is refused with no reply, the connection is closed, and one rate-limited handler: refused ... line is logged.
  • A mismatched declaration gets {EFS_ERR_PROTO, 3} and the connection is closed. This also applies on an already-declared connection.
  • Every efsd connection opener declares first:
    • efs-fuse: the pool declares before the RDMA upgrade. Discovery (LIST_NODES) and the mount bootstrap (RAFT_STATUS) declare too.
    • Daemon peer pool: declares before the RDMA upgrade and before the HELLO/build-id join gate. Joins, Raft and forwards all use this pool.
    • efs-mgmt: every command uses efs_connect_declared. The status probe declares under its own 2 s bound.
    • Tests: the live and measure C programs, the raw-socket Python live tests and scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh all declare.
  • These openers are exempt:
    • Reachability probes in node_cache.c connect and close without sending anything.
    • tests/perf/tcp_rdma/xprt_bench and the self-hosted unit tests (test_rdma_xprt, test_rdma_segmented, test_data) are their own server, not efsd.
  • scripts/w125_p3_compat.sh now expects old clients to be refused and exits nonzero otherwise.
  • Gates:
    • tests/test_declaration_gate.c PASS on efs3 (TCP frame path). It covers undeclared requests refused without a reply, HEARTBEAT, wrong, short and bad-magic declarations, an accepted declaration followed by a served request, and client-side refusal.
    • tests/test_declaration_gate_handler.py PASS. It checks the handler ordering and that every opener declares.
    • The RDMA frame path of the same test is NOTRUN on efs3 (no IB device).
    • make test on efs3 (Fedora 42, aarch64, TMPDIR on disk), every command run independently: 874 of 875 PASS. The one failure, tests/test_reclaim (t_basic put assertion), fails identically on devel 19555889f on efs3, so this branch did not cause it.
    • Fake-server and handler-slice tests now answer or stub the declaration (test_gc_status_expiry.py, test_expiry_cli.py, test_node_left_refused.py).
    • The cluster refusal run (w125_p3_compat.sh) is NOTRUN.

<a id="w138"></a>

W138 — test_apply_ring.py succeeds while its TSan check is NOTRUN on gcc 11

Verification correctness; opened 2026-10-21 from the audit T5; FIXED on devel-k25 (October 22).

  • On gcc 11.5.0 (node9901) the TSan build failed: 'atomic_thread_fence' is not supported with '-fsanitize=thread' [-Werror=tsan] (src/server/apply_ring.h:38, :61).
  • The test prints SKIP and passes (tests/test_apply_ring.py:229–231), so the race check and its negative control never run on the build node.

Fix and gate: fix the test, not the synchronization.

  • The ring payload already uses atomics, and the fences carry the seqlock ordering.
  • -Wno-error=tsan can enable a diagnostic run, but TSan does not model the fences, so a clean run is not proof.
  • Keep the torn-record stress check and the negative control, record the sanitizer's limits, and report SKIP as NOTRUN.
  • Any change to the memory ordering needs its own correctness review.

Fix (October 22, devel-k25, alpha K25), test only, no change to apply_ring.h:

  • The TSan half runs or the test fails with the reason; there is no SKIP path left. A build failure (including a missing libtsan) and a binary that does not run both exit nonzero with the compiler or runtime output.
  • gcc's 'atomic_thread_fence' is not supported with '-fsanitize=thread' is allowed with -Wno-error=tsan for the sanitizer build only, and only after the plain build reported it (clang does not); the fences stay.
  • The limit is in the PASS line: TSan does not model the fences, so a clean run covers the atomic payload accesses, not the ordering; the torn-record stress check (4 M native writes, 3 readers, 0 torn) is the ordering gate. The TSan builds use 400 k writes. The plain-field negative control still runs and must be reported as a data race.
  • Verified: Mac/clang PASS; efs3 gcc 15.0.1 aarch64 PASS after libtsan was installed there (the gcc build without the retry does fail -Werror=tsan, so the retry path is exercised). node9901 gcc 11: NOTRUN here, expected to take the same path.

<a id="w140"></a>

W140 — The proposal RPC accepts metadata tags this build cannot apply

Correctness / safety; opened 2026-10-22 from the W127 gate; fix on devel-k02 (8b8048a5b), unit gates PASS on efs1; cluster gate NOTRUN.

  • EFS_MSG_RAFT_MKFS with a payload (server_raft_host_submit) refuses only reserved and retired tags (EFS_MD_CMD_IS_RESERVED). Any other byte is proposed and committed.
  • Since W127, every replica refuses such an entry at apply and the group stops serving until it is reformatted. So one request from any connection can halt a metadata group.
  • Shown by scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh on node9901 (tag 200 to group 0, October 22).

Fix (8b8048a5b, October 22):

  • include/efs/meta_cmd.h carries EFS_MD_CMD_APPLIED, the table of log commands this build applies, and efs_md_cmd_applicable(). It is the one source of truth: host_apply_dispatch checks it before any handler (the final EFS_ERR_UNSUPPORTED halt stays for anything a handler cannot decode), and host_tag_refused() refuses every other tag with EFS_ERR_PROTO at the top of host_propose_impl, the only function that appends to a Raft log. The submit RPC, the inode RPC handlers, background reclaim, the packer (server_raft_host_pack_propose) and forwarded commands all end there. One log line per second, with the count of refusals suppressed in between.
  • tests/test_submit_unknown_tag.py (in make test): the dispatcher compares against exactly the table's 48 tags, every log append is behind the gate, the predicate over all 256 values, and the production gate in front of a real single-voter Raft log: tag 200 (and reserved, retired, RPC-only and CFG tags) answer PROTO with the log and applied count unchanged, the next CREATE commits at the next index, the log line is rate-limited. tests/test_meta_cmd_namespace.py checks the table names every EFS_MD_CMD_* but host-only CFG and no EFS_MD_REQ_*.

Remaining gate:

  • Cluster: tag 200 to group 0 through the proposal RPC answers PROTO, the group's log and applied index do not move, and the group keeps serving. scripts/w127_incompatible_entry.sh can no longer plant an incompatible entry through the RPC; the W127 B1-B4 gate needs another vehicle (a log entry written below the gate) before it is rerun.
  • Who may submit at all is W133 (connection-state matrix); this item only closes the encoding hole.

All 13 items are worth tracking; they are not 13 demonstrated product bugs. Review of the items introduced by e681ff97e; documentation only, no fixes or new runtime qualification. Existing OPEN/NOTRUN verdicts remain unchanged.

ItemsAssessment
W127–W130Confirmed unsafe apply behavior by code inspection. Preserve legitimate business refusals while fixing malformed-command and storage-error handling; cluster reproduction gates remain NOTRUN.
W131Defensive hardening with runtime reachability unproven, not a demonstrated running-cluster failure.
W132–W133Confirmed unsafe endpoint and protocol-enforcement gaps; declaration is not authentication.

W138–W139Qualification gaps scoped to the audited environment/default suite. Absence from that suite does not mean a test cannot run manually or through a dedicated target.

Keep the separate W numbers for traceability, but implement W127–W131 as one coherent apply-hardening package with shared error classification and real apply-boundary tests. W132 can proceed independently. W133 requires the connection-state matrix; W134 requires the W72 integration, not an isolated removal of its bypass.

Do not assign identical release-blocker status to all 13. Prioritize live correctness/enforcement issues and trustworthy qualification of enabled paths. Staged-feature tests may be removed when that feature is archived coherently; this must not remove coverage of a still-exposed server endpoint. Qualification must distinguish PASS, FAIL and NOTRUN, including environment-dependent checks. Any release decision still needs the named acceptance results; this review does not waive gates, close items, or authorize a release. No additional conceptual review is needed before implementation against these requirements.

<a id="w143"></a>

W143 — efs-fuse reads diagnostic environment switches on per-op paths

Performance; opened and closed 2026-10-22 (both gates recorded); deployed in 46496416e. Verified: getenv is gone from both clients' on-CPU profiles under the same load. make test 816/816 with one environmental failure (docs check without results/). Found by passively profiling orcd-mini on 08cc16af4 under two tiny_files.py writers (profile). On the node9901 client, getenv was 2.9% self and 3.7% with children of efs-fuse on-CPU time. __strncmp_evex and __strlen_evex, used by getenv's environment scan, added another 1.8% and 1.1%. On node9900 it was 1.3% on 2026-10-21. getenv walks the whole process environment on every call. These checks read diagnostic switches that never change after start:

  • EFS_RPC_PROF in dir_lock_take: every directory lock, and 64 times per efs_client_lock_all_dirs (once per stripe) on the eviction path;
  • EFS_RPC_PROF in lookup_memo_observe (every lookup) and efs_append_flush_report_run (every flush);
  • EFS_OPID_TRACE_VERBOSE and EFS_OPID_TRACE in inode_rpc.c: several per create, lease and append;
  • EFS_STAGE_DBG per eviction pass.

Fix. Each of the 20 affected functions reads its switch once into a function-local static int (-1 until read), as write.c already does for EFS_REPORT_DBG. The cache stays inside the function: source-slice tests compile these functions alone, and an earlier version that used a shared header helper and file-scope caches broke 14 of them. Unchanged: startup-only reads, error-path EFS_RDMA_FIRST logging and EFS_FAULTS-only checks. Behaviour is unchanged, because no test or tool sets these variables at runtime.

Gates.

  • make test on node9901 (scripts/make_test_summary.sh). Many tests compile slices of the changed files.
  • A client on-CPU profile under the same tiny-file load shows getenv below 0.1%.

The client is not the throughput limit here: both mounts used only 0.16–0.18 cores. The gain is efs-fuse CPU, not create rate.

<a id="w144"></a>

W144 — LOOKUP/GETATTR on a group follower takes h->mu for the leader hint

Performance; opened and closed 2026-10-22 (both gates recorded); deployed in 784bcc6ee. Verified with split leadership (n3 led group 0, n2 led group 2): host_namespace_leader_hint no longer appears in the leaders' lock waits. make test 816/816 with one environmental failure. Found in the orcd-mini profile on 46496416e (profile, p2). There, leadership was split: n2 led group 0 and n1 led group 2. On n1, host_namespace_leader_hint ← host_read_leader_hint ← server_raft_host_lookup was the largest lock-wait site: 22.1% of n1's lock-wait switches, ahead of proposals.

The function routes LOOKUP, GETATTR and namespace mutations to a dual-group leader. When this node is not the group's leader, it took h->mu to read both groups' committed voters. The 2026-10-18 profile saw nothing, because then one node led both groups and the leader returns before locking.

Fix. Read the voters with host_route_voters, the lock-free published view also used by host_leader_cover_pick: the raft voters for a hosted group, else the slot's atomically stored set. A group without a local slot still yields no hint, as before. The hint can be one pump cycle old, which was already true, and the recipient rechecks authority. tests/test_namespace_leader_route.py gets the matching stub; all its assertions are unchanged and PASS. test_host_cover_route and test_query_target_route PASS.

Gates.

  • make test on node9901.
  • After deploy, with split leadership, host_namespace_leader_hint is gone from the leader-node lock waits. One node leading both groups does not exercise the path.

<a id="w145"></a>

W145 — A follower commits its own unproven log tail after an InstallSnapshot

Raft safety; opened 2026-10-22. Root cause fixed and deployed (76614e8e8); orcd-mini n2 repaired 16:20Z with efs-mgmt raft-resync. The four remaining parts are fixed or answered on branch devel-k01 (no client was acknowledged for 30,929,219@62); orcd-mini deploy gate NOTRUN. Seen on orcd-mini (784bcc6ee, two tiny_files.py writers, ~16 M files) after a 3 s perf --call-graph dwarf capture stalled the group-2 leader n2 at 12:54:41–44Z (profile, p4).

What happened. The sequence is reconstructed from the three nodes' raft.log files: a read-only record scan of each group's ENTRY, TRUNC, HARD, SNAP and CFG records.

  1. n2, as term-62 leader, appended entries 30,929,219–30,929,230 in term 62. They reached neither n1 nor n3.
  2. n1 and n3 ended term 62 at 30,929,218. n1 won term 63 and wrote its no-op at 30,929,219 in term 63; n3 holds the same.
  3. n2 stepped down to term 63. n1 then sent it an InstallSnapshot of n1's 12:41 snapshot (index 30,676,477; n2 logged CFG and SNAP last=30676477/54).
  4. n2 had already applied past that index, so it took the "already applied" branch, snap_installed(…, take_cfg=0). That branch ends with commit_index = min(leader_commit, last_i), where last_i is the follower's own log tail. n2's tail still held its unreplicated term-62 entries. n2 committed and applied 30,929,219@62 at 12:54:49Z, three seconds after n1 and n3 had committed 30,929,219@63.
  5. The leader walked n2's tail back one truncation per round trip (TRUNC from=30929230 … 30929220). At 30,929,219 the conflict sat at n2's commit index. on_ae_req returns EFS_ERR_PROTO with no reply there, and the pump discards that result, so the walk-back stopped.

From then on n1 resent the same window every heartbeat. With W145's diagnostics deployed, n2 showed proto_drops rising by about 20/s (AE conflict at index=30929219 <= commit=30929219 … refused without reply), and n1 showed next=30929220, match=0 and reject_hint=30929219 for peer 1.

Consequences.

  • n2's group-2 state machine applied an entry the cluster never committed.
  • Reads routed to n2 wait (read-sleep/apply-sleep at 400 ms).
  • Open check: the entry (command tag 1) was proposed at n2. If n2's waiting proposer saw it applied with a matching term, a client may have been told that an operation succeeded which the cluster never committed.

Fix (source).

  • snap_installed may advance commit_index only to min(leader_commit, incl). The snapshot proves its own last index and nothing after it, and a matching AppendEntries proves the tail.
  • tests/test_raft.c test_snapshot_commit_stops_at_snapshot replays n2's case. It FAILs on the old code: the stale tail commits and applies, and the leader's replacement cannot land. It PASSes with the fix.

Diagnostics added (22a2207cd, plus election and step-down lines):

  • raft-status shows each group's last log index and term, snapshot index, rejects sent and protocol drops. On the leader it shows each peer's next/match index, in-flight batch and age, ACK age, batches sent/refused/blocked/failed, and rejects with their hint.
  • Follower refusals log every 10 s; silent PROTO refusals always log; oversize inbox frames are counted.
  • Elections, votes, step-downs (with the commit quorum and match table) and any commit by a non-leader are logged.
  • scripts/w145_deposed_leader.sh reproduces deposition on a private cluster; its SIGSTOP and perf modes passed without reproducing.

Deployed 76614e8e8 on orcd-mini (2026-10-22 14:22Z):

  • make test 816/816 with one environmental failure; POSIX smoke 216/216; 3/3 identical versions.
  • The first swap left n3 on the old build: stop.sh did not stop it, and start.sh then refused n2. The cluster was down about 14:20–14:22Z until a second clean stop and start. The swap script now refuses to switch until every efsd has exited.
  • Startup elections moved group 2 from term 149 to 291. The cause is not yet examined.
  • As expected, n2 is still wedged: its committed 30,929,219@62 is on disk, and proto_drops keeps rising. The fix prevents new cases; it does not repair n2.

n2 repair (2026-10-22, with the user's go-ahead).

  • No existing path could make a leader send n2 a snapshot, so 613bb2c78 added the operator-only efs-mgmt raft-resync.
  • The first attempts exposed two more bugs:
    • W146: images over 4 GiB could not be imported;
    • W147: a transfer restarted on every send while the leader committed.

Both were fixed (e75391268, a569de971).

  • On a569de971, raft-resync 10.1.99.1:17433 2 (16:15:59Z) led n3 to send its 5.2 GB image. n2 imported it as a full diff (3,769,881 keys) and installed it at index 33,953,093 (16:20:33Z), replacing its stray 30,929,219@62.
  • Afterwards all three nodes were at group-2 commit and applied 33,967,666, the request had cleared, n2 logged no read-sleep/apply-sleep, and POSIX smoke was 216/216.
  • Each deploy restart took about 3 minutes, because n2's shutdown waited for a handler stuck in a group-2 read and stop.sh gave up on the remaining daemon. The guarded swap script retried.

Remaining.

  1. Find why the new leader sent a 4.7 GB snapshot to a follower that was only a few entries behind, instead of walking its tail back.
    • Likely cause: any rejection with match_index 0 (for example a stale-term reply) resets the leader's next_index to 1, below its log floor.
  2. Check whether a client was acknowledged for index 30,929,219@62.
  3. Every restart today ran hundreds of elections: group 2 went from term 511 to 721 to 923 to 1121.
  4. A daemon blocked in a group read delays its shutdown past stop.sh's wait. stop.sh then leaves the remaining daemons running.

K1 follow-up (branch devel-k01, status note).

  1. Snapshot to a near follower: fixed in 48d14a37d. The new leader's first commit/read probe went out with prev_index 0; its success reply (match 0) set next_index to 1, below the log floor. A success now never lowers next_index, and a prev-term conflict hints below the whole uncommitted run of the conflicting term. Unit tests FAIL on the old code and PASS with the fix.
  2. Acknowledged write: not acknowledged. All 26 n2 waits on 30,929,219–30,929,230 ended at the 400 ms deadline with applied=30929217/30929218 (12:54:45.943–46.986Z), so their handlers returned BUSY. n2 applied the stray 30,929,219@62 at 12:54:49Z, over two seconds later. A verdict needs applied >= idx inside one bounded wait and a matching term; no caller re-waits on the same (index, term). The clients logged only successful retries. n2's raft.log no longer holds the record (replaced by the 16:20Z resync); the efsd and fuse logs still cover the window.
  3. Restart election storms: fixed in dd876e069 with pre-vote. A node campaigned alone from the moment its groups started until its peers listened (n3: term 923 -> 1120 in 33 s, then deposed the leader). The vote/election/step-down lines are rate limited per group. Unit tests FAIL on the old code and PASS; on a private efs1 cluster a staggered restart moved terms 1 -> 20/18 before and 1 -> 2 after.
  4. Blocked handler at stop: fixed in 781df5750. A pooled RDMA client kept one handler serving retried group reads (no quorum while peers stopped); TCP SHUT_RD does not reach the RDMA channel. Handlers now close before the next request once a stop begins, and the drain is bounded at 40 s (refuse, log, exit rc 3 without teardown). Unit test PASS; the RDMA case was not reproduced on a cluster.

Gates.

  • make test PASS (done).
  • orcd-mini deploy, with n2 back in sync after its repair (done, 16:20Z).
  • A private reproduction of deposed leader + snapshot under load, with the deposed leader catching up and no stale commit.

<a id="w146"></a>

W146 — A snapshot image over 4 GiB can never be installed

Correctness/liveness; opened and closed 2026-10-22. Deployed in e75391268. Gate PASS: n2 installed the 5.2 GB group-2 image on orcd-mini (16:20Z; import diff of 3,769,881 keys). Found while repairing W145 on orcd-mini. The group-2 snapshot image is 5.2 GB (group 0's is 5.4 GB). A follower installing it reads both the incoming and its local image whole through read_whole, which refused any file over 0xffffffff bytes with EFS_ERR_NOMEM. Every install failed after the transfer (raft-snap: import diff group=2 rc=-2 n=0), and the leader re-exported and re-sent the 5.2 GB image about every 45 s. Any follower that falls below a leader's log floor at this scale could never catch up.

Fix. read_whole, parse_image and efs_kv_group_import_prepare use 64-bit image lengths and offsets. The image format is unchanged: a 32-bit entry count and 32-bit key and value lengths. The import still holds both images in memory, about 10 GB for group 2 on orcd-mini. test_kv_lsm, test_kv_snapshot_tail, test_raft_store and test_raft PASS. make test 816/816 with one environmental failure. A unit test with an image over 4 GiB is too heavy for the suite; the gate is a live install.

Gate. An InstallSnapshot of an image over 4 GiB completes on orcd-mini (the W145 n2 repair).

<a id="w147"></a>

W147 — A snapshot transfer restarts on every send while the leader commits

Liveness; opened and closed 2026-10-22. Deployed in a569de971. Gate PASS: n2's group-2 transfer completed on orcd-mini while the group committed, with no re-export. Found while repairing W145 on orcd-mini.

  • The group-2 leader's stored snapshot point (30,676,475) had no file. Its snap-2-*.kvx had been rotated away; a restart keeps only the index.
  • In that case send_snap re-exported at the current applied index on every call. The group kept committing, so each export got a new index, the peer's transfer offset reset to 0, and a new 5.2 GB image was exported about every 45 s.
  • n2's partial file stalled at 46 MB. Any follower needing a snapshot at this scale would see the same, as long as the group commits during a transfer.

Fix. When the stored snapshot point has no file and a newer image is already open whose index is still in the log, send_snap keeps sending that image. It re-exports only when no usable image is open.

While a W145 resync is requested, the follower's "prev beyond log" rejection also carries match_index 0. Its untrusted tail must not pull the leader out of the transfer and back into the conflicting AppendEntries.

tests/test_raft.c test_snap_transfer_survives_commits: a restarted leader whose snapshot file is gone transfers a multi-chunk image while committing between chunks.

  • On the old code: FAIL (the transfer never completes; one export per send).
  • With the fix: PASS (the transfer completes with at most two exports).

Gate. n2's group-2 InstallSnapshot completes on orcd-mini (the W145 repair, together with W146).

<a id="w150"></a>

W150 — No test for the abandon scan's work-budget stop and resume

Test coverage; opened 2026-10-22 from the packing validate-once review; FIXED on devel-k25 (October 22).

  • efs_pack_abandon_scan (src/meta/pack_mapping.c) is bounded by efs_kv_lsm_scan_work, which counts tombstones. A stop by that budget resumes after the work cursor, not the callback's last live key.
  • tests/test_pack_validate_once.c drove only callback stops on the memory store, so the work-cursor path, a tombstone-only window and the term restart had no test.

Fix (test only, no change to the scan). abandon_sweep_work_bound runs on an LSM store with 48 objects of four owner/state kinds, interleaved with 0–16 flushed-then-deleted generations each, before the first object and after the last. Each bounded call checks that the budget counts tombstones and that the cursor strictly advances or wraps. The test also covers:

  • one pass finds every actionable object exactly once; the first window holds tombstones only, and the budget stops most windows;
  • wraparound: the next pass finds the same set again;
  • mutation mid-pass: an object ahead is cancelled and a new one admitted, and the pass reports exactly the current set;
  • term change: continuing the old cursor misses this node's earlier admissions, and the packer's restart finds them all in one pass;
  • budget edges: a budget equal to the measured key count wraps in one call; one key short stops just before an actionable last key, and the next window reports it and wraps.

Check that it catches defects (efs3, then reverted). A scan that drops the work cursor fails the new case at the cursor-advance check. That mutation passes the old memory-store cases. An inclusive resume fails both. Gate: make test on efs3, in the K25 report.

Raw evidence note (2026-10-23): the bulk data in gc-buffered-3ohdte4d (copied stores, generated payloads and build trees) was deleted. Text logs, results and profiler captures remain under /data1/efs/evidence/, each with a PRUNED.txt listing what was removed. Reproduce the bulk with the method on this page.

Appendix 6 — Naming

Source: how-it-works/naming.md (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to docs/how-it-works/). Authority: normative protocol.

Naming intent. The bar for this design is that it earns the idea of an "extreme filesystem": it scales as close as possible to the raw hardware. Every design decision is checked against that bar — a component is wrong if it serializes work the hardware could have done in parallel.

On the name itself. "extremfs" is close in spelling and sound to the existing XtreemFS project, whose site attributes its trademark registration to Quobyte. "EFS" is also the name used for Amazon Elastic File System. These primary-source identity checks were made Oct 7, 2026; they do not establish trademark clearance or quantify search-engine dominance.

A distinctive, searchable public name remains a design goal, deliberately open pending a proper name/search check. This project continues to use "efs" as its working name; this review does not choose or approve a replacement. Earlier wording is preserved.

Appendix 7 — Design rationale

Source: how-it-works/design-rationale.md (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to docs/how-it-works/). Authority: rationale (explains the index; never overrides it).

This is the rationale document: why the architecture in architecture.md has the shape it has, what is claimed and what is not, and what was deliberately rejected. The spec itself is normative; this file argues for it. Accepted design reasoning is not an implementation or release certificate; the public-path matrix and named acceptance records define the current limits.

Let's be precise about what is and isn't claimed. Raft-per-shard over an embedded KV is not a new mechanism. The claim is stronger than novelty: the design is a consequence of the constraints, and the argument is a derivation, not an analogy. A copy-cat cites a working system and imitates it. A derivation starts from what must be true and shows which shapes survive.

The constraints are forces, not preferences

ConstraintForce it exertsDesign it eliminates
2³² objects on 4 nodes~512 GiB+ of metadata cannot live in RAMthe former fully-in-RAM table
immediate cross-client visibilityno authoritative cache may go staleTTL / negative / attr caches as truth
survive f nodes down, read and writea write must commit without the dead nodessingle-coordinator 2PC, primary-backup without failover
3 → 64 nodeswork must spread, not funnel to one writera single cluster-wide metadata primary
scale with raw hardwareparallel work must not hit a software serializerwhole-table flush; per-write inode-row mutation

The constraints strongly favor one family; efs picks proven primitives within it

The constraints do not mathematically force "Raft + ordered KV" specifically — Multi-Paxos or Viewstamped Replication, and a B-tree or LSM or custom page store, satisfy the same forces. The honest statement:

The constraints strongly favor a partitioned replicated state machine with persistent, paged applied state. efs chooses Raft and an ordered embedded KV because they satisfy those requirements with proven, understandable primitives and minimal new protocol invention.

That this is also where Ceph and CockroachDB landed is not imitation — it is convergent evolution. The same forces act on any strongly-consistent, horizontally-scaled, fault-tolerant store, so independent systems solve the same equations and arrive at the same shape. Convergence is evidence the derivation is correct, not that it was copied.

The safety properties are inherited theorems plus explicit composition obligations

  • Core shard-replication safety is inherited from Raft when implemented according to its assumptions (election restriction, log matching, commit rules, safe reconfiguration). Leader completeness (I2) is Raft's theorem, not majority intersection alone.

D36 overrides the earlier node-count ladder. Three nodes are minimum; four provide the maximum two-loss safety target; larger clusters add scale. Majority Raft alone cannot meet the four-node requirement. Its replacement/composition proof remains open; never weaken the target to match current implementation.

  • Quorum durability (I10/I11): a majority-acknowledged write survives any failure that leaves a majority. With RF = 2f+1 that tolerates f losses within the Raft failure envelope, provided the durable-ACK and storage assumptions are actually satisfied. The production fragment barrier remains W71; Raft quorum math alone does not certify those writes.
  • EFS-specific composition is not covered by Raft's proof. RPC dedup, KV persistence ordering, cross-shard transaction logic, FUSE cache coherence, EC generation publication, chunk RMW, reconfiguration, and the orphan lifecycle remain explicit proof / model / simulation obligations. That is exactly what the simulator is for.

What is genuinely ours — stated precisely

Let us be exact about the claim, because overclaiming here would be both wrong and unsupportable. Every primitive in this design has existed: Raft, distributed metadata, RDMA, erasure coding, immutable generations, ordered KV stores, directory sharding, deterministic simulation. Several systems illustrate individual parts. Primary-source pointers checked Oct 7, 2026 provide context, not an exhaustive prior-art search or comparative ranking:

  • WEKA's current cluster overview describes drive, compute, frontend and management processes distributed across server containers. That description does not by itself prove every earlier claim about hash placement or complete POSIX semantics.
  • DAOS DFS/dfuse documentation describes its POSIX namespace/API and currently lists hard links and flock among limitations. This is a versioned interface statement, not a claim that EFS already implements all those semantics or that future DAOS releases cannot.
  • VAST's architecture white paper describes disaggregated shared-everything storage and shared metadata/ transaction state; it is a different architectural composition.
  • CephFS metadata documentation distinguishes client-direct RADOS data access from MDS-managed inode and directory metadata. An MDS role need not imply dedicated physical hardware.
  • GIGA+ and the IndexFS paper precede this design's incremental large-directory spreading.
  • FoundationDB's testing documentation describes deterministic cluster simulation alongside live and hardware tests. Simulation alone is not physical fault acceptance.

Earlier unsourced comparison wording is preserved. We are not claiming to have invented these mechanisms.

The claim is the composition and the governing principle. What we have sought is this combination as one open POSIX filesystem; the following is a design goal, not proof that no existing public system has the same composition:

POSIX namespace
  + no dedicated MDS tier
  + metadata authority distributed across ordinary storage nodes
  + Raft only for small authoritative metadata state
  + client-direct RDMA data path
  + k+f EC immutable chunk generations
  + no whole-file serialization for parallel writers
  + no inode serialization where independent chunks can proceed
  + directory locality until it becomes a bottleneck
  + failure correctness designed before performance tuning
  + deterministic protocol simulation
  + small-cluster simplicity

And the principles that tie it together — the things that, if we execute them, are the actual contribution (§0 of the spec):

P1 · Never serialize work that the semantics and the hardware allow to happen in parallel. P2 · Co-locate what must commit atomically on the common path; distribute what can evolve independently. P3 · Make stale work harmless instead of trying to prevent it.

Traditional PFS architectures handle 1000 clients → 1000 different files well. The hard problem is 1000 clients → ONE file → different byte/chunk ranges. efs's answer is that if writes do not conflict, the filesystem must not invent a conflict merely because they share an inode: disjoint chunks publish to different metadata shards (see the data protocol), size is a sharded high-water mark co-located with the chunk it extends (P2), sub-chunk RMW is generation CAS, stale publications are fenced by content epochs rather than prevented (P3), and only the operations whose semantics require serialization (O_APPEND EOF allocation, overlapping byte ranges, truncate, rename) are serialized — because the semantics demand it, not because the filesystem happens to have one inode lock.

That is a thesis strong enough to build a filesystem identity around. It is also falsifiable: if a workload that the hardware could parallelize is found to serialize in efs, that is a bug against this principle, and it is the simulator's and the benchmarks' job to find it.

The namespace is the database

A second, quieter part of the identity. Traditional filesystems hand you a namespace and leave you to build find, du, crawlers, inode scanners, cron lifecycle jobs, and external catalogs around it. But efs metadata is already a distributed ordered database. So the questions operations actually asks — largest files, files owned by X, files older than Y, everything under project Z, storage consumed by a directory, data whose TTL expired — should be metadata queries, not filesystem traversals:

du         = a query over the ordered KV, not a namespace walk
find       = a range scan / index lookup, not a crawl
expiration = an indexed metadata operation, not a cron forest

The namespace metadata is the database; there is no separate catalog bolted on and derived from periodic snapshots. This is a natural consequence of the metadata design, not an extra subsystem — and it is part of what "minimalist" means operationally (below).

Stated honestly, this is a thesis the architecture makes possible, not a mechanism it already specifies. The base keys — (parent,name) and (ino) — efficiently answer lookup, getattr, and readdir. They do not by themselves answer "all files owned by uid 1000", "everything older than 30 days", or "all .bam files > 1 TiB" without scanning billions of inode rows; and du /project/foo is genuinely hard because subtree membership is hierarchical. Making find/du/TTL real queries requires one of: secondary indexes (which must stay consistent with inode mutation — another same-shard co-location or transactional-indexing decision, P2), distributed materialized aggregates (per-subtree size/count maintained incrementally), or query-time parallel shard scans (the KV is ordered and sharded, so a full scan at least parallelizes across all 4096 shards instead of walking a tree serially). The architecture's commitment is narrower and real: namespace-wide questions are answered without walking the POSIX namespace, because the data is already in a queryable distributed store. The derived-index design is a separate, explicitly-scoped follow-on.

Minimalism as a design constraint

What may distinguish efs as much as any algorithm is operational simplicity:

3 servers  ->  install  ->  efs init  ->  efs mount  ->  done
64 servers ->  the same architecture

No metadata servers to provision, no metadata-target sizing exercise, no hierarchy of special node types, no weekly du, no crawler database, no lifecycle cron forest, no kernel module, no twenty-component deployment. Delivering that and serious performance and strong POSIX semantics is the goal. The architecture serves it: ordinary storage nodes are the metadata consensus participants, so there is nothing extra to operate.

The thesis in one line: the constraints force the family, Raft + KV are the proven primitives within it, and the part that is ours — the composition, the never-serialize-what-can-run-parallel principle, and the namespace-as-database minimalism — is where the design earns an identity.

What is deliberately rejected

  • Millions of tiny consensus groups beyond the shard count. 4096 groups is the ceiling; more re-creates the catchup-storm class.
  • MVCC / multi-version metadata. Not required by the current filesystem semantics and intentionally omitted. The Raft log gives mutation order; it is not a substitute for MVCC. Introduce MVCC only if future snapshot, scan, or cross-shard transaction semantics require versioned reads.
  • A second storage path for metadata pages. Everything goes through the same log + KV. (Two-paths-diverge has bitten twice.)
  • Client-side metadata caching for correctness. Caches may exist for performance but are never authoritative (and the kernel cache is actively invalidated — see the FUSE contract in architecture.md).
  • Kernel module. Stay on FUSE; the low-level (inode-based) FUSE API migration is a separate, orthogonal client rewrite.
  • Clock-based leader leases on the authoritative read path. Clocks are not correctness inputs.
  • Hard-disk support. EFS is flash/NVMe-only (§1 hardware envelope of the spec). No seek-aware layouts, no rotational-latency hiding, no SMR handling — the design spends the assumptions flash makes true (cheap random I/O, deep hardware queues, µs-scale device latency) instead of defending against disk.
  • An N = 2f durability-only mode. Permanent majority loss is disaster territory, not an operating mode — see failure-tolerance.md for why a survivor-log merge cannot be made safe by prose.

Appendix 8 — Failure tolerance — derivation

Source: how-it-works/failure-tolerance.md (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to docs/how-it-works/). Authority: normative protocol (derivation of the index's tolerance table).

Implementation scope: this page specifies the accepted design, not a current deployment guarantee. The public-path review records persistence, session, fixed-profile/repair and integrity limitations; consult those gates before claiming this contract is implemented.

Architecture · Design rationale · Data protocol

The normative node-count contract lives in §2 of the spec, accepted as D36 on Oct 9: three nodes minimum, four nodes maximum two-loss protection, larger clusters for scale. This supersedes the previous f=3 ladder. The mathematics below explain a limitation of majority Raft; they must not be used to silently replace the accepted four-node requirement with five nodes. The required four-node metadata protocol is unresolved and not implemented.

The derivation

The two planes scale differently with the configured failure target f (maximum two simultaneous permanent node losses under D36):

  • Data (EC): a k+f stripe survives any f losses (any k of k+f fragments reconstruct). Needs N ≥ k+f distinct failure domains.
  • Metadata (Raft): a committed entry lives on a quorum Q = ⌊RF/2⌋+1. Zero data loss through f permanent losses needs every committed entry to keep at least one surviving copy (Q > f), and the system staying authoritative with no human in the loop needs the survivors to still form a quorum: N − f ≥ Q. With RF = N (every node carries every shard's replica in the small-cluster limit) that is N ≥ 2f+1. More generally RF = 2f+1 replicas per shard, placed on distinct failure domains, gives Q = f+1 and survival of any f replica losses with both properties.

For f=2, ordinary majority Raft needs five voting failure domains for continued authority. D36 requires preservation with four nodes, so selecting a different metadata protocol and its safe recovery behavior is mandatory before claiming compliance. No extra node or witness is implicitly authorized.

Why survivor-log merge does not implement the four-node requirement

At N = 2f exactly (e.g. 4 nodes wanting f=2), f permanent losses leave a minority of survivors. Every committed entry still has ≥1 surviving copy (Q + f > N), so the bits survive — but plain Raft cannot re-establish authority without a majority, and no local merge rule over the surviving logs can reconstruct the committed prefix. Commitment information died with the majority.

The tempting merge — "per log index, the highest-term entry wins" — is unsound. Raft's log-prefix properties hold only within logs produced through Raft; they do not license constructing a new log by independently selecting entries per index. A legal sequence is an old-term uncommitted branch followed by a current-term quorum commit on another prefix (as in Raft §5.4.2, Figure 8). The older Y becomes committed when Z is committed in term 11; Y was not committed in term 9. For four voters A/B/C/D: B initially stores Y alone; A wins term 10 with C/D and stores X alone; B wins term 11 with C/D and commits Y→Z on B/C/D. A remains isolated. Permanent loss of C/D then leaves these two survivors:

survivor A:   index 5  term 10  X        (uncommitted branch)
survivor B:   index 5  term 9   Y        (initially uncommitted)
              index 6  term 11  Z        (quorum-committed in term 11,
                                          committing Y with it; A stayed
                                          isolated from that majority)

The merge produces X@5, Z@6 — a log that never existed. Z was created on a prefix containing Y, not X. Worse, the merge drops Y, which was committed and possibly acknowledged to a client. Operation-ID idempotency does not fix this: the problem is not duplicate application but a synthesized state-machine history no leader authorized.

Raft is deliberately majority-based; the paper provides availability only while a majority remains, and production systems (e.g. etcd) treat permanent quorum loss as disaster recovery, not ordinary log reconciliation. This rules out the former survivor-log-merge recipe, not D36. Four-node/two-loss preservation is now required and needs a separately proved metadata protocol. Current Raft cannot advertise that guarantee.

Profile migration obligations (metadata recipe needs D36 review)

The cluster carries effective_f (the guarantee currently in force) and, during a change, target_f. Raising f:

  1. add shard replicas via joint consensus (safe reconfiguration, §7.1 of the spec);
  2. complete the profile cutover barrier — the control plane enters PROFILE_CUTOVER(P+1), pushes P+1 to every publication authority, and waits for each to durably ACK it. From that point publication validation (data protocol) rejects any new publication whose durability evidence is not on the target profile, so the set of old-profile current generations can only shrink;
  3. re-stripe every protected data generation published before the cutover to the new k+f width — each re-striped chunk is a new immutable generation written under the new coding profile (coding_profile_id), never an in-place reinterpretation of an existing generation;
  4. verify that no current generation remains on the old profile;
  5. only then commit effective_f = target_f.

Step 2 is a barrier that must reach the authorities that enforce it. A control-plane Raft commit does not change what 4096 independent lane leaders believe; a leader still holding profile P will happily accept an old-profile publication after the "cutover", and the scan below is then verifying a set that is still growing. This is exactly the mistake session fencing had before round 7 — an authority cannot enforce a decision it has never been told about — so coding_profile_id/profile_epoch is installed shard-local configuration, replicated through each shard's own Raft group, and the barrier is complete only when every publication authority has ACKed:

control plane commits PROFILE_CUTOVER(P+1)
push P+1 to every publication authority
every authority durably ACKs           <- barrier complete
only now begin the old-profile scan

Without the barrier the scanner races live writers and the verification is meaningless:

scanner re-stripes chunk X to 2+2
scanner moves on
    client publishes a NEW generation of X, still 2+1     <- allowed
scanner finishes, "verified"
effective_f := 2        -- but the current X survives only 1 loss

Because the cutover is committed before the scan and publication validation enforces the current profile (round 7), any generation created after the barrier is already on the target profile, and the scan only has to cover generations that existed before it — a set that cannot grow. That is what makes "no current generation is on the old profile" provable rather than merely observed. In-flight writers holding the old profile are rejected at publication and retry on the new one; their fragments are orphans (L7), which is P3 working as intended.

The guarantee changes at that final commit, not when the operator asks.

Lowering f is not the same sequence run backwards. Raising works because the weaker guarantee stays advertised while stronger data accumulates — every intermediate state is at least as safe as what was promised. Lowering inverts that: switching new writes to the weaker profile first would publish 2+1 data while the cluster still advertises f=2, so the advertised guarantee would be false for as long as the migration takes. The advertised guarantee must therefore drop first:

LOWERING f:  2+2  ->  2+1
1. commit effective_f = target_f (the weaker guarantee)   <- advertise first
2. profile cutover barrier to the weaker profile (as above)
3. re-stripe / allow old wider generations to age out
4. only then shrink metadata RF and release replicas

Metadata RF comes last in both directions for the same reason: replicas are removed only once nothing depends on the stronger quorum, and added before anything does.

Re-striping must not touch user-visible metadata. It rewrites a generation's representation, not the file's content, so it never updates size, mtime or ctime — a migration that silently restamped mtime on every chunk it re-encoded would corrupt every incremental-backup and make-style workflow on the system while reporting success. The same rule applies to repair/rebuild. Both are placement changes, not reformats. EC stripe width k is independently configurable (wider k on larger clusters trades encode CPU for storage efficiency. The default remains 2+2 above four nodes; a wider profile is not an accepted default. Data placement needs k+f distinct domains; the metadata mechanism must independently meet D36.

Degraded operation

While the cluster is already operating with u unavailable failure domains (u ≤ f failures already consumed), a data generation may publish with D ≥ k + (f − u) durable fragments, marked degraded and queued for repair — the invariant "survives the remaining f−u further losses" is maintained throughout. The full rule is in the data protocol; rebuild scheduling is in performance.md.

u is protection debt, not a headcount — repair pays it back, a node coming back does not. It is tempting to define u as "domains currently down" and recompute it as nodes return. That is wrong, and it silently under-protects data:

f = 1, k = 2 (2+1)
A unavailable                       -> u = 1
generation G publishes to B, C      -> degraded, legally (k + f-u = 2)
A returns                           -> "u = 0"?  A does not hold G
B dies                              -> G has one fragment, k = 2
-> acknowledged data lost after ONE failure, at f = 1

The returning node restores capacity, not the missing fragments, so the budget it appears to give back was never re-earned. u is therefore defined per generation as outstanding protection debt: a degraded generation consumes budget from the moment it publishes until its missing fragments have actually been reconstructed and made durable. Aggregate degraded debt is what the control plane reports and what admission for further degraded publication is checked against; only repair retires it. This is also why repair is prioritized above rebuild-for-balance (performance.md) — debt is a live reduction of the advertised guarantee.

Unavailability is a committed control-plane state, never a client's timeout. Degraded publication is allowed only against domains the control plane has decided are unavailable and recorded as such; it is never used because a target is merely slow. In an asynchronous network a client cannot distinguish the two, and letting it try would let any latency spike quietly lower the protection level of freshly written data.

Appendix 9 — Protocol — cross-shard transactions

Source: how-it-works/protocols/transactions.md (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to docs/how-it-works/). Authority: normative protocol.

Implementation scope: this is the accepted transaction protocol. Namespace and resize primitives exist; request-wide public data publication and observation remain W77. Do not infer FUSE activation from the presence of metadata transaction helpers. Decision retirement (W83) follows the GC rule below; namespace predicate bounds remain W84; coordinator authority also depends on the read-freshness gate W82.

Architecture · Data protocol · Directory protocol · Sessions

The operations that genuinely touch more than one shard (see the operation→participant matrix in §6 of the spec: mkdir/rmdir, cross-dir rename, hardlink, unlink with nlink>1 or with the dentry on a different shard than the inode, and every multi-lane atomic write()) need atomic visibility, which a reconcile rule alone does not provide. efs uses a Raft-backed distributed transaction — decentralized, no global transaction server:

txid (stable across all participants)
coordinator = participant[hash(txid) % participant_count]
participant set

PREPARE  -> each participant writes a durable intent
DECISION -> coordinator Raft-commits COMMIT | ABORT (durable)
RESOLVE  -> participants apply/abandon per the decision

The coordinator is dispersed by txid, not pinned to a fixed participant: this protocol is on the hot write path (every multi-lane write() uses it — see the data protocol), and a large file's writes repeatedly touch the same lane set — a deterministic-per-file coordinator would re-create a same-file serializer. Hashing the txid spreads decision records across the file's own lane leaders, so independent write transactions never funnel into one shard.

Atomic commitment is only half the problem. The other half is concurrency control — without it, two concurrent transactions over the same keys (rename(a,b) vs unlink(a); rename(a,b) vs rename(a,c)) have no serializable history even though each commits atomically.

  • Conflict detection at PREPARE. A prepare is conditional: prepare(T, key, expected_version). It fails if another live transaction holds a conflicting intent on key, or if key's current version no longer equals expected_version (the key changed since the transaction read it). An intent on an exclusive key is that key's lock: at most one live transaction holds it.
  • Not all transaction state is an exclusive key — and getting this wrong silently re-creates the hotspot one level down. A transaction's effects split into kinds, and only the first kind takes an exclusive lock:
  exclusive / CAS keys        the chunk-map entry, a dentry, an inode row
                              -> conflict, version check, one holder

  commutative reductions      MAX(lane.max_end,   ...)
                              MAX(lane.max_mtime, ...)
                              MAX(lane.max_ctime, ...)
                              MAX(dir_lane.mtime, ...)
                              -> transaction PAYLOAD, not a lock

  read / predicate guards     lane_seq · dentry_seq · parent_version ·
                              content_epoch · mtime_gen
                              -> SHARED: many guards coexist; a guard
                                 conflicts with anything that would change
                                 the guarded state, through the decision

Consider two writers publishing chunk 10 and chunk 74 of one file, which by construction share a write lane (data protocol). They conflict on nothing: different chunk-map keys, and MAX commutes. If the transaction machinery treated (FileID, lane) as an exclusive intent key because both transactions update the lane's high-water marks, they would conflict anyway — and the per-file serialization the lanes were introduced to remove would simply have moved from the inode to the lane. So reductions are carried in the intent and applied by the reducer at resolve time; they never block a prepare. Several live transactions may hold reduction payloads on the same lane concurrently, provided their exclusive keys are disjoint. This is P1 applied to the transaction layer itself.

"Not a lock" must not mean "not visible." A reduction still becomes effective at its transaction's decision, and the decision can precede the reducer materializing it into lane.max_end:

  lane.max_end = 1 GiB
  T publishes at 2 GiB; T's COMMIT decision is durable
  T's intent has not been resolved yet; lane.max_end is still 1 GiB
  stat() reads lane.max_end -> 1 GiB          -- WRONG: T already returned

So a lane's reduction state is not just its materialized marks. Pending reduction intents are stored discoverably under the lane's own key prefix, and the authoritative read of a lane is

  effective(lane.max_X) = MAX( materialized lane.max_X,
                               reduction payloads of pending intents on this
                               lane whose decision resolves to COMMIT )

resolved by the same four-state rule below. Materialization by the reducer is therefore a background compaction of already-visible state, never the event that makes a committed reduction observable. Because the pending set is bounded by the in-flight transactions on that lane, this is a short scan, and it is what makes I21 hold end to end rather than only at the moment of commit.

  • Read/predicate guards: the third primitive, and several protocols are unsound without it. A transaction frequently needs an observation to stay true until it decides — not a value it intends to write. Checking a version at prepare time is not enough on its own, because the gap between the final check and the decision is exactly where the observation can be invalidated. So a guard is a real, durable, shared participant record:
  guard(T, key, observed_version)
      -> succeeds alongside other guards on the same key
      -> conflicts with any mutation that would change that key's state
      -> is held until T decides, not until T finishes reading

Guards are what make these protocols correct, and they are the same mechanism in every case, which is the point of naming it once:

  O_APPEND reservation   guards the active lanes' lane_seq  (§7.3)
  RMDIR on a HASHED dir  guards each dentry shard's dentry_seq
  directory rename       guards every ancestor's parent_version (§7.4)
  stat() / read fallback guards the collected lane / chunk-map versions

The RMDIR case also needs the guard to cover things that do not exist yet — the classic phantom. Emptiness is a statement about a range, and an empty range contains no key whose version could be checked:

  RMDIR: shard 17 holds no entries of this directory   -> "empty"
  CREATE: inserts `foo` into shard 17
  RMDIR: commits on its earlier observation
  -> a directory removed while an entry existed

A version check over the existing keys cannot see this, because the conflicting write created a key that was not there to be checked. The fix is to give the predicate a materialized witness: every directory carries a dentry_seq per dentry shard, bumped by every dentry mutation on that shard including inserts. RMDIR guards those sequence keys, so the CREATE above conflicts with the guard and one of the two aborts. This gives predicate-level isolation without MVCC and without a distributed entry counter (rejected in directory.md — a counter rebuilds the per-directory hotspot that spreading exists to remove).

  • No-wait, and what that buys. A prepare that finds a conflicting intent fails immediately — nobody ever waits while holding an intent, so no wait-for cycle can form and deadlock is impossible by construction. The loser aborts its acquired intents and retries with randomized backoff (livelock is bounded by backoff/priority tuning, a liveness knob, not a correctness mechanism). Because no-wait already gives deadlock freedom, prepares do not need sequential acquisition:
    • Write-publication transactions (hot path): all PREPAREs are sent in parallel (P1 — the transaction must not serialize what the hardware can do concurrently).
    • Namespace transactions (rare): participants and keys are prepared in a canonical global order (by shard id, then key) — a simple, deterministic schedule that minimizes retry churn for the rename/unlink/link family.
  • Visibility rule. An intent is never externally visible as a committed effect; readers that encounter an intent resolve it against the coordinator's decision, so clients never observe an illegal intermediate (I17). A transaction becomes visible at its decision, not when background cleanup happens to run — a reader that meets a decided-but-unresolved intent must reflect the decision, or a client could fail to see its own just-returned write. Resolution has exactly four outcomes, and the last one is a safety rule, not an error path:
  authoritative COMMIT        -> the new value
  authoritative ABORT         -> the old value
  authoritative NO-DECISION   -> the old value; this read linearizes before
                                 whatever the decision turns out to be
  cannot establish authority  -> retryable error (EIO/EBUSY). Never guess,
                                 and never report the effect as absent.

The fourth line is I9 again, in transaction clothing: unknown because unreachable must never be answered as not there.

  • Idempotency / retry. The whole transaction carries one txid; re-prepare and re-resolve are idempotent (I16).
  • Crash recovery. A recovering participant or a reader that finds an intent queries the coordinator's durable decision and drives the transaction to completion (L5).
  • GC. Resolved intents are reclaimed (L7-class). A decision record outlives its intents — a recovering participant must still be able to ask what happened — so it has its own explicit retirement rule (W83):

A decision is retirable once every participant's RESOLVE has been applied in that participant's group log with an OK verdict; it is then retired by a replicated TXN_RETIRE command on the coordinator's group, which keeps a verdict-bearing tombstone that is reclaimed only by a later TXN_RETIRE whose logged clock is at least the retention (60 s) past that tombstone's retirement. An absent decision whose txid is not newer than the shard's replicated reclaim floor is unknown: readers refuse it as retryable BUSY and a late DECIDE is refused, so a reclaimed verdict is never answered as the old value or re-minted.

  DECIDE  [txid][coord][dec][participants]   live record = verdict + parts
  RESOLVE on every participant               each verdict OK -> proof
  TXN_RETIRE [txid][coord][now]              live -> tombstone(verdict, now)
                                             + reclaim <= 32 tombstones with
                                               now - retired_at >= 60 s,
                                               resuming at a stored cursor;
                                               floor = max txid time reclaimed
  lookup(txid): live | tombstone -> verdict
                absent, txid time >  floor -> NO-DECISION (undecided)
                absent, txid time <= floor -> UNKNOWN (STALE -> reader BUSY,
                                              DECIDE refused)

Every input of the rule is replicated state or a field of the logged command (the proposer's clock rides in TXN_RETIRE), so all replicas delete the same keys at the same log index; no replica deletes on a local timer. Both commands decode exactly: DECIDE is 23 + 4·n bytes with a COMMIT or ABORT verdict, 1 ≤ n ≤ 144 distinct in-range participant shards and an in-range coordinator; TXN_RETIRE is 29 bytes with an in-range coordinator. Any other entry (short, trailing bytes, invalid field) is refused before the store is touched and halts the group through the unsupported-entry path (W127). A well-formed DECIDE with the other verdict is a transaction conflict (PROTO verdict to the proposer), not malformed. Each apply touches a bounded window (one live record, at most 32 tombstones, one cursor/floor record), so retirement cannot stall the apply loop. The proposer of a transaction (its RESOLVE wait, the finisher, or recovery) proposes TXN_RETIRE after the last RESOLVE verdict. If that proposer dies or its RETIRE is lost, the decision stays live — never deleted by age — and the recovery sweep re-drives RESOLVE to the participants recorded in the decision and then retires it. The sweep reads each coordinator shard's live decisions one page per pass from a per-shard continuation cursor (at most 32 records and 256 examined keys, LSM deletion tombstones included), resumes after the last key it examined and wraps to the prefix start at the end. A decision whose participants cannot resolve stays live and is met again on the next round, so it never hides the decisions after it. The cursor is the leader's volatile hint, not replicated state: after a restart or a leadership change the sweep starts at the prefix beginning. A shard stays due for sweeping until one page that covered the whole prefix from its start finds no live decision. Retention must stay at least 10× the 5 s recovery age (a compile-time check in the host), so a verdict outlives recovery and proposer clock skew. Recovery that meets an UNKNOWN decision for a pending record knows every RESOLVE already applied, so the record is a straggler PREPARE and is dropped on that shard only. A transaction whose txid time trails the floor (clock skew beyond the retention) cannot decide and is aborted: fail-closed. Retained state is therefore live decisions of unretired transactions plus one retention window of tombstones per coordinator shard, not completed operation history. Duplicate-suppression records have the matching bound in sessions.md.

With conditional prepare + no-wait, the protocol yields strict serializability for multi-shard ops: conflicting transactions are ordered by intent acquisition, non-conflicting ones run concurrently.

Terminology. What the old design deleted is the global root-snapshot 2PC durability mechanism — the one whose commit point was an insufficiently-replicated coordinator/root-generation. A per-operation Raft-backed 2PC-like protocol for cross-shard transactions is a different thing and is exactly what's needed here. Raft (replicated ordering within a shard) and 2PC (atomic commitment across shards) solve different problems; efs uses each where it fits.

Appendix 10 — Protocol — data plane

Source: how-it-works/protocols/data.md (headers demoted, nav stripped, links rebased to docs/how-it-works/). Authority: normative protocol.
